This page reproduces the models presented in Chapter 20 in Chan et al. (2019). Each example follows the structure laid out in figure 12.4 in the book.

Load required packages

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(bvartools)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(spam)
library(tidyr)
```


## Exercise 20.1: The vector autoregressive model with independent normal-Wishart

### Prepare data

US macro data until 2007Q4

```{r data, fig.width=5, fig.height=4.5, message=FALSE}
# Specify URL
url <- "https://web.ics.purdue.edu/~jltobias/second_edition/Chapter20/code_for_exercise_1/US_macrodata.csv"
# Load data
us_macro_2007 <- read.csv(url, col.names = c("date", "Dp", "u", "r"))
# Omit NA values
us_macro_2007 <- na.omit(us_macro_2007)
# Transform into time-series object
us_macro_2007 <- ts(us_macro_2007[, -1], start = c(1959, 2), frequency = 4)

# Generate data matrices for estimation
temp <- gen_var(us_macro_2007, p = 2, deterministic = "const",
                iterations = 5000, burnin = 1000)

# Reset random number generator for reproducibility 
set.seed(8472376)
```

### Set priors

```{r}
object <- add_priors(temp,
                     coef = list(v_i = 1, v_i_det = 1 / 10),
                     sigma = list(df = "k + 3", scale = 1))
```


### Estimate

In this example only the initial values of the variance-covariance matrix have to be set. They are based on the OLS estimator.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, results='hold'}
ex_20_1 <- draw_posterior(object)
ex_20_1 <- thin(ex_20_1) # Thin the output
```

Obtain impuse response functions as in figure 20.1

```{r irf, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=3.3, message=FALSE}
# Calculate impulse responses
Dp <- irf(ex_20_1, impulse = "r", response = "Dp", n.ahead = 20, type = "oir", keep_draws = TRUE)
u <- irf(ex_20_1, impulse = "r", response = "u", n.ahead = 20, type = "oir", keep_draws = TRUE)
r <- irf(ex_20_1, impulse = "r", response = "r", n.ahead = 20, type = "oir", keep_draws = TRUE)

# Obtain means
Dp <- colMeans(Dp)
u <- colMeans(u)
r <- colMeans(r)

# Prepare for plotting
temp <- cbind(Dp, u, r) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(time = 1:n() - 1) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c("Dp", "u", "r")) %>%
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("Dp", "u", "r"),
                       labels = c("Inflation", "Unemployment", "Interest rate")))

# Plot
ggplot(temp, aes(x = time, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free")
```

Although qualitativly equal, the values of the IRF differ, since `bvartools::irf` does not allow to set the size of a shock yet.

## Exercixe 20.2: Vector autoregression with Minnesota prior

### Prepare data

We use the same data set as in Exercise 20.1. although with lag $p=1$.

```{r}
# Generate data matrices for estimation
temp <- gen_var(us_macro_2007, p = 1, deterministic = "const")
y <- temp$data$Y
x <- temp$data$Z

# Generate further variables
k <- NROW(y) # Number of endogenous variables
tt <- ncol(y) # Number of observations
z <- kronecker(t(x), diag(1, k)) # SUR form
m <- ncol(z) # Number of estimated coefficients
```

### Set prior hyperparameters

Since function `bvartools::minnesota_prior` uses a slightly different formula to calculate the prior covariance matrix, the prior hyperparameters need to be adapted to be consistent with the prior hyperparameters used in Chan et al. (2019). See `?minnesota_prior` for the formula.

```{r}
temp <- minnesota_prior(temp, kappa0 = .5, kappa1 = .5, kappa3 = 200)

# Priors of coefficients
mu_prior <- temp$mu # Prior mean
v_i_prior <- temp$v_i # Prior variance
sigma_i <- temp$sigma_i # OLS estimate of the inverse error covariance matrix
```
  
### Posterior results
  
Since the Minnesota prior allows for an analytical solution, there is no need to use the Gibbs sampler.
  
```{r}
# Posterior variance 
v_post <- solve(v_i_prior + t(z) %*% kronecker(diag(1, tt), sigma_i) %*% z)

# Posterior mean
a_post <- v_post %*% (v_i_prior %*% mu_prior + t(z) %*% kronecker(diag(1, tt), sigma_i) %*% matrix(y))
```
  
The posterior means are:
  
```{r}
# Obtain rounded values in matrix form  
a_mean <- round(t(matrix(a_post, k)), 3)

# Name rows and columns
dimnames(a_mean) <- list(dimnames(x)[[1]], dimnames(y)[[1]])

# Look at result
a_mean
```

And the posterior standard deviations are:

```{r}
# Obtain rounded values of in matrix form
sd_mean <- round(t(matrix(sqrt(diag(v_post)), k)), 3)

# Name rows and columns
dimnames(sd_mean) <- list(dimnames(x)[[1]], dimnames(y)[[1]])

# Look at result
sd_mean
```

The results are pratically identical to the values presented in the book. The lower standard deviation of the interest rate coefficient in the interest rate equation should be a typo.

## Exercise 20.5: Stochastic search variable selection in VARs

### Prepare data

We use the same data set as in Exercise 20.2.

```{r}
# Generate data matrices for estimation
temp <- gen_var(us_macro_2007, p = 1, deterministic = "const",
                iterations = 20000, burnin = 2000)
```

### Priors

```{r}
object <- add_priors(temp,
                     sigma = list(shape = 0.01, scale = 100),
                     ssvs = list(inprior = .5, tau = c(.01, 100), errors = TRUE))
```

### Obtain posteriors

The `bvartools` package's own posterior simulation function `bvaralg` includes functionality to draw posterior draws as described in the Chan et al. (2019). In this regard, note that the second edition of the book contains some errors in section 20.5, which were corrected for the implementation. The MATLAB code of the book is correct as well.

The following adjustments were made to the hyperparameters used to obtain draws of the variances $\psi_{ii}^2$.

* The hyperparameter $\overline{a}_i = \underline{a}_i + \frac{T}{2}$.
* The hyperparameter $ \overline{b}_j = \underline{b}_j + \frac{1}{2} \left\{ s_{jj} - s^{\prime}_j \left[ S_{j - 1} + \left( \underline{D}^{\eta}_j \right)^{-1} \right]^{-1} s_j \right\} $

Beside that it should be noted that the hyperparameter $\overline{b}_i$ is a *rate* parameter.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hold'}
ssvs_result <- draw_posterior(object)
```

### Results

```{r}
summary(ssvs_result)
```

The results are very similar to the results in the book. Differences might result from different random number generation, which could also lead to slightly different inclusion probabilities.




## Exercise 20.6: Time varying parameter VAR

### Data: US macro data until 2007Q4

```{r, echo=FALSE}
rm(list = ls())
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Specify URL
url <- "https://web.ics.purdue.edu/~jltobias/second_edition/Chapter20/code_for_exercise_5/US_macrodata.csv"
# Load data
us_macro_2007 <- read.csv(url, col.names = c("date", "Dp", "u", "r"))
# Omit NA values
us_macro_2007 <- na.omit(us_macro_2007)
# Transform into time-series object
us_macro_2007 <- ts(us_macro_2007[, -1], start = c(1959, 2), frequency = 4)

# Genenerate data matrices
temp <- gen_var(us_macro_2007, p = 2, deterministic = "const")
y <- temp$Y
x <- temp$Z

k <- nrow(y) # Number of endogenous variables
tt <- ncol(y) # Number of obs
m <- nrow(x) # Number of regressors
n <- m * k # Number of estimated coefficients
```

### Estimation

Priors

```{r}
# Initial conditions
a0_mu_prior <- matrix(0, n)
b0_v_i_prior <- diag(1, n)
diag(b0_v_i_prior)[n - k + 1:k] <- 1 / 10 # Prior for determinsitic terms

# Priors for measurement equation errors
sigma_df_prior <- k + 3
sigma_df_post <- tt + sigma_df_prior
sigma_scale_prior <- diag(1, k)

# Priors for state equation errors
q_shape_prior <- 3
q_shape_post <- q_shape_prior + tt / 2
q_rate_prior <- rep(.01^2, n)
q_rate_prior[n - k + 1:k] <- .1^2 # Determinsitic
```

Initial values

```{r}
y_vec <- matrix(y)

z <- matrix(0, k * tt, n * tt)
for (i in 1:tt) {
  z[(i - 1) * k + 1:k, (i - 1) * n + 1:n] <- kronecker(t(x[, i]), diag(1, k))
}
z <- as.spam(z)

beta0 <- tcrossprod(y, x) %*% solve(tcrossprod(x))
sigma_temp <- tcrossprod(y - beta0 %*% x) / tt
sigma_i_temp <- solve(sigma_temp)
sigma_i <- kronecker(diag(1, tt), sigma_i_temp)
sigma_i <- as.spam(sigma_i)

beta0 <- matrix(beta0)

q_i <- kronecker(diag(1, tt), diag(100, n))
q_i <- as.spam(q_i)

h <- diag(1, m * k * tt)
diag(h[-(1:(m * k)), 1:(m * k * (tt - 1))]) <- -1
h <- as.spam(h)
```

Gibbs sampler

```{r}
iterations <- 21000
burnin <- 1000

# Data containers for draws
draws_beta <- NULL
for (i in 1:tt) {
  draws_beta[[i]] <- matrix(NA, n, iterations - burnin)
}
draws_sigma <- matrix(NA, k * k, iterations - burnin)

# Start Gibbs sampler
for (draw in 1:iterations) {
  # Draw parameters
  HQiH <- crossprod(h, q_i) %*% h
  XSi <- crossprod(z, sigma_i)
  K_beta <- HQiH + XSi %*% z
  mu_beta <- matrix(solve(K_beta, HQiH %*% kronecker(matrix(1, tt), beta0) + XSi %*% y_vec))
  beta <- mu_beta + solve.spam(chol(K_beta), rnorm(n * tt))
  
  # Measurement eq. variance-covariance matrix
  u <- matrix(y_vec - z %*% beta, k)
  sigma_i_temp <- rWishart(n, sigma_df_post, solve(sigma_scale_prior + tcrossprod(u)))[,, 1]
  sigma_i <- as.spam(kronecker(diag(1, tt), sigma_i_temp))
  
  # State eq. error variances
  beta <- matrix(beta, n)
  v <- apply(beta - cbind(beta0, beta[, -tt]), 1, function(x) {sum(x^2)})
  q_post <- cbind(q_shape_post, q_rate_prior + v / 2)
  q_i_temp <- apply(q_post, 1, function(x) {rgamma(1, shape = x[1], rate = x[2])})
  diag(q_i) <- rep(q_i_temp, tt)
  
  # Initial condition
  K_beta0 <- b0_v_i_prior + q_i[1:n, 1:n]
  mu_beta0 <- solve(K_beta0, b0_v_i_prior %*% a0_mu_prior + q_i[1:n, 1:n] %*% beta[, 1])
  beta0 <- mu_beta0 + solve(chol(K_beta0), rnorm(n))
  
  # Save draws
  if (draw > burnin) {
    pos_draw <- draw - burnin
    
    for (i in 1:tt) {
      draws_beta[[i]][, pos_draw] <- as.matrix(beta[, i])
    }
    
    draws_sigma[, pos_draw] <- solve(sigma_i_temp)
  }
}
```

### Impulse responses

Create `bvar` obejcts for further analysis

```{r}
# For 1975Q1
tt_1975 <- which(time(us_macro_2007) == 1975) - 2
bvar_1975 <- bvar(y = y, x = x,
                   A = draws_beta[[tt_1975]][1:(n - k),],
                   C = draws_beta[[tt_1975]][n - k + 1:k, ],
                   Sigma = draws_sigma)

# For 2005Q1
tt_2005 <- which(time(us_macro_2007) == 2005) - 2
bvar_2005 <- bvar(y = y, x = x,
                   A = draws_beta[[tt_2005]][1:(n - k),],
                   C = draws_beta[[tt_2005]][n - k + 1:k, ],
                   Sigma = draws_sigma)
```

Obtain impulse responses for inflation

```{r Dp, fig.width=4, fig.height=3.5}
irf_1975 <- irf(bvar_1975, impulse = "r", response = "Dp",
                n.ahead = 20, type = "oir", keep_draws = TRUE)

irf_2005 <- irf(bvar_2005, impulse = "r", response = "Dp",
                n.ahead = 20, type = "oir", keep_draws = TRUE)

# Difference between the IRF
diff_irf_Dp <- irf_2005 - irf_1975
diff_irf_Dp <- t(apply(diff_irf_Dp, 2, quantile, probs = c(.05, .5, .95)))
diff_irf_Dp <- diff_irf_Dp %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(var = "Inflation",
         time = 1:n() - 1)

# Mean IRF
irf_1975 <- colMeans(irf_1975)
irf_2005 <- colMeans(irf_2005)

irf_Dp <- cbind(irf_1975, irf_2005) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(var = "Inflation",
         time = 1:n() - 1)
```

Obtain impulse responses for unemployment

```{r u, fig.width=4, fig.height=3.5}
irf_1975 <- irf(bvar_1975, impulse = "r", response = "u",
                n.ahead = 20, type = "feir", keep_draws = TRUE)

irf_2005 <- irf(bvar_2005, impulse = "r", response = "u",
                n.ahead = 20, type = "feir", keep_draws = TRUE)

# Difference between the IRF
diff_irf_u <- irf_2005 - irf_1975
diff_irf_u <- t(apply(diff_irf_u, 2, quantile, probs = c(.05, .5, .95)))
diff_irf_u <- diff_irf_u %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(var = "Unemployment",
         time = 1:n() - 1)

# Mean IRF
irf_1975 <- colMeans(irf_1975)
irf_2005 <- colMeans(irf_2005)

irf_u <- cbind(irf_1975, irf_2005) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(var = "Unemployment",
         time = 1:n() - 1)
```

Obtain impulse responses for interest rate

```{r r, fig.width=4, fig.height=3.5}
irf_1975 <- irf(bvar_1975, impulse = "r", response = "r",
                n.ahead = 20, type = "feir", keep_draws = TRUE)

irf_2005 <- irf(bvar_2005, impulse = "r", response = "r",
                n.ahead = 20, type = "feir", keep_draws = TRUE)

# Difference between the IRF
diff_irf_r <- irf_2005 - irf_1975
diff_irf_r <- t(apply(diff_irf_r, 2, quantile, probs = c(.05, .5, .95)))
diff_irf_r <- diff_irf_r %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(var = "Interest rate",
         time = 1:n() - 1)

# Mean IRF
irf_1975 <- colMeans(irf_1975)
irf_2005 <- colMeans(irf_2005)

irf_r <- cbind(irf_1975, irf_2005) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(var = "Interest rate",
         time = 1:n() - 1)
```

Figure 20.2: Mean IRF

```{r, message=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
temp <- bind_rows(irf_Dp, irf_u, irf_r) %>%
  # Bring it into long form
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("irf_"),
               names_to = "Period") %>%
  # For better labelling in the plot
  mutate(var = factor(var, levels = c("Inflation", "Unemployment", "Interest rate")),
         Period = factor(Period, levels = c("irf_1975", "irf_2005"),
                         labels = c("1975", "2005")))

# Plot
ggplot(temp, aes(x = time, y = value, colour = Period)) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free") +
  geom_line() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank())
```

Figure 20.3: Plot differences between IRF

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
temp <- bind_rows(diff_irf_Dp, diff_irf_u, diff_irf_r)
names(temp) <- c("ymin", "y", "ymax", "var", "time")

temp <- temp %>%
  mutate(var = factor(var, levels = c("Inflation", "Unemployment", "Interest rate")))

# Plot
ggplot(temp, aes(x = time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = "a"), alpha = .3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = y, colour = "a"), show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free")
```
